positioning: The Irish farmhand with a silk coat and a spring in its step.
story: Most terriers wear armor. The Wheaten wears silk. That one difference tells you where it came from and how it behaves.
The breed began on Irish farms, where a dog had to earn its supper. It herded cattle, guarded the house, and cleared the barn of rats. Nobody bred it for a show ring. Nobody had the time.
Its coat is the trademark. Soft, wavy, and the color of ripening wheat, it sheds little and tangles easily. Puppies are born darker. The wheat color comes with age.

The temperament is a terrier’s, turned friendly. A Wheaten is busy, bold, and bright. It is also the one terrier that greets strangers like old friends. Owners call it the Wheaten greetin’, a bouncing hello that can reach the top of a doorframe.
That bounce needs exercise. A bored Wheaten invents its own jobs, and you will not approve of them.
Give it a walk, a brush, and a family. You get sunny, sturdy devotion with the energy of a farm dog and the heart of a lapdog.
fblocks: Named for its soft, wheat-colored coat, rare among terriers. It was the all-purpose working dog of the Irish farm.
It shares ancestry with Ireland’s other terriers but trades the harsh jacket for silk. The Irish Kennel Club recognized it in 1937.
Lively and outgoing. Needs daily exercise and company. The coat needs regular brushing to avoid mats. Low-shedding, which many owners prize.
A single coat, soft and gently waving, in shades of wheat from pale beige to gold. Dark puppy coats clear as the dog matures.
Seventeen to nineteen inches tall. Recognized by the AKC in 1973. Five or six puppies to a litter.
days: Rain on the window, a warm stove, and an old dog with nothing left to prove.
A Wheaten has a single soft coat. No woolly undercoat, so it sheds little.
Irish farm dogs worked from dawn to dusk. The Wheaten herded, guarded, and ratted.
Wheaten puppies are born dark. The wheat color arrives slowly, often by age two.
When the day is too much, put your head in a boot and wag. It helps.
The Irish Kennel Club recognized the Wheaten in 1937. The AKC followed in 1973.
A basin, a wool blanket, and a heap of sleepy puppies. Farm life at its best.
last_walk:
The door is open, and the lantern is lit.
A Wheaten greets the end of the day the way it greeted the start. Tail up, ears forward, sure that something good is coming. Old Seamus sits on the step and watches the first stars. Tomorrow there will be another hello.
